The prevention sciences graduate certificate combines skills with methods to understand how to reduce risk and promote health and healthy development.
There is an emphasis on examining social determinants of health with the aim of enhancing equity and decreasing disparities.
Additionally, this program provides intellectual development and training to a diverse community of students who can benefit from foundational and applied skills in health promotion and disease prevention but require flexible academic pathways (Strategic priority 2; Goal 1; Action 1).
This certificate can be completed to meet requirements in the Master's of Professional Studies program and the Master's of Public Administration program.
For the Master's of Professional Studies (30 credits total), students complete two certificates, and six additional credits of coursework.
The Prevention Science certificate can be included as one of the certificates toward completion of the degree.
For the Master's of Public Administration (36 credits total), students complete three certificates to complete the degree.

The Prevention Science certificate can be included as the third certificate the students complete towards their degree.
The certificate could also be taken as a stand-alone certificate for any interested students.
One of the key elements of prevention science is the partnership with key community stakeholders (both public and private) who can work together to develop and implement appropriate interventions that address today’s health-related challenges.
Using evidence-based practices, applied learning, and real-world scenarios, students will be able to explore a range of issues through the lens of promoting and protecting health (e.g., social justice, family trauma, substance abuse and/or other addictions).
Therefore, the interdisciplinary nature of the program aims to foster meaningful interactions amongst students who bring expertise from a variety of health backgrounds.

This program aligns with the URI strategic plan priorities and goals in several ways to include: 1) Strategic Priority 1 (Broaden Our Impact), Goal 1: Contribute to broad and deep impacts on the social, cultural, and economic ecosystems across Rhode Island, the nation, and beyond. 2) Strategic Priority 2 (Enhance Student Achievement), Goal 2: Increase graduate student enrollment and degree completion. 3) Strategic Priority 4 (Power the University of the Future), Goal 4: Expand research and new academic programs and services through an increased focus on revenue generation.

With 38 states allowing medical cannabis and 23 states now having adult use markets, legal cannabis has become the fastest growing industry in the United States.
The legal cannabis workforce has tripled over the past five years, outpacing the height of the technology sector's job growth.
Cannabis retail sales are estimated to reach $33.6 billion in 2023 with an additional economic impact of $100.8 billion.
These estimates do not include the hemp nor cannabidiol (CBD) markets that have grown out of the federal legalization of cannabis containing less than 0.3% tetrahydrocannabinol (THC).
The rapid job growth represents a problem for employers and has created public health concerns due to the lack of qualified employees.
The graduate certificate in cannabis sciences aims to address these concerns by providing students with the current knowledge in cannabis pharmacology and skills in cannabis formulation, manufacturing, and analysis.
Graduates of the certificate will have the knowledge to evaluate, develop, and research cannabis products in terms of safety and function.

Specifically, graduates will be able to 1) relate concepts of pharmacology and pharmaceutics to the development and therapeutic use of cannabis products, 2) propose strategies for the development of safe, stable, and functional cannabis products that meet or exceed current regulatory frameworks, and 3) apply analytical and bioanalytical techniques to assess the quality of cannabis products and the presence of cannabis metabolites in biological matrices for pharmacological studies.
The certificate program aligns with the University's mission and Strategic Plan by aiming to be an innovator in cannabis science education.
Specifically, the certificate addressed Priority 1: Broaden our Impact by providing students with the skill and knowledge necessary to make meaningful impacts and drive innovation in the cannabis field by adding to the scientific understanding of cannabis, solving challenges with product safety and stability, and addressing the stigma of cannabis through rigorous scientific inquiries (Goal 1 Action 2).

This will be accomplished by exploring current evidence-based literature and immersing students in the real world techniques and processes of cannabis and related industries (Goal 2 Action 3).
Priority 2: Enhance Student Achievement will be meet by the program through the use of interactive teaching technologies, the design of active learning discussions and assignments, and the implementation of andragogical strategies (Goal 1 Action 1).
The certificate is being offered in the accelerated 7 week format through URIOnline making it accessible to working professionals, those seeking career advancement or change, and other nontraditional graduate students (Goal 1 Action 2).
The program is designed as a stand alone certificate, but also has the potential to form the technical component of a new professional science master's (PSM) degree (Goal 2 Action1).
The certificate will enable the RI workforce to meet the challenges of the expanding medical and recreational cannabis market in RI and provide an opportunity for alumni to gain expertise in the evolving field aligning with Priority 3: Foster an Inclusive Culture (Goal 1 Action 3).

Finally, for Priority 4: Power the University of the Future , the certificate will generate new revenue streams in three ways: as a new academic program, by creating four new online courses, and as the technical component of a new PSM degree to be proposed in the future (Goal 4 Action 1).

The science of pharmaceutical development is essential to the process of bringing a therapeutic entity from compound discovery to treatment in humans.
Most importantly, it seeks to create dosage forms for the compound that are safely consumed by humans (and animals), are stable until ingested, release the active drug product efficiently, avoid detrimental biologic interactions, have a consistent response, and have a known and controllable safety profile.
Advances in the knowledge and uses of injectable, biotech products have added a significant complexity to the drug development process.
In comparison to small molecule drug products, biological molecules have four levels of structure considerations making the development process much more complex and challenging.
Currently, over 70% of the compounds in the bio/pharmaceutical insudstry's drug development pipeline are large biological molecules.
This is a rapidly evolving area mandating continued education for those holding entry level degrees.
Graduates will have the knowledge to design and articulate a whole team approach to the product life cycle of a candidate drug molecule from initial identification through commercial launch.

Specifically, students completing this on-line certificate program will be able to 1) Describe the design and challenges of the pharmaceutical product development process from initial concept to market as well as the roles and responsibilities of each operational group; 2) Implement cGMP regulations for pharmaceutical drug substance and drug product manufacture; and 3) Develop product development strategies to optimize the creation of novel pharmaceuticals in industrial settings.
The online Graduate Certificate in Pharmaceutical Development meets the Provost's academic priority for active e-learning via technology-enhanced pedagogy and online programs.
Further, italigns with key goals of URI's 2022-32 Strategic Plan.
One goal of this Plan is to enhance studentsuccess by equipping learners with skills that are in demand in an ever-changing world, which this proposed certificate program aims to achieve.
The Pharmaceutical Development certificate program also addresses this goal's strategy of facilitating the implementation of new learningpedagogies and the expansion of modes of course delivery and assessment by leveragingspace and time in new ways.

This program also addresses the Plan's goal for diversity and social justice, as the Certificate program curriculum will include strategies for reducing genetic disparities in drug design, and for optimizing the use of pharmaceutical development resources to programs that serve vulnerablepopulations.
Additionally, this certificate program will augment knowledge in health and the STEM sciences, and develop the workforce to enhance public safety, as described in the Plan's goal to expand research, scholarship, and creative work.

CASC Procedures

The Curriculum and Standards Committee (CASC) Procedures CASC examines course and program proposals to ensure they are comprehensible and user-friendly for undergraduate students.
Within the Kuali proposal, we examine all ﬁelds to conﬁrm clear details vital to student success, such as prerequisites, course rationale and description, the number of seats and sections offered per year, and syllabi.
Syllabi should accompany all major course proposals (new classes, signiﬁcant modiﬁcations to a course).
To ensure proposal syllabi will be clear to students, we look for: ● straight-forward course information (class description & objectives, method of instruction); ● clear course policies, structures, and methods of teaching; ● clarity regarding grade scale & methods, assignments, and how coursework connects to credit hours; ● current information about accessible technological resources and apps necessary for the class; Further, students are best served by having up-to-date information on support services such as DAI; illness policies; and procedures reﬂecting current University standards.
Where these items are overlooked or out-of-date, CASC may provide friendly feedback.

Also, ATL has resources and templates for syllabi ( https://web.uri.edu/atl/design/syllabus/ ).
New courses should provide supporting documentation uploaded by the chair of the department/academic unit into the proper Kuali ﬁeld, indicating the date that their department/program voted to approve the course.
Program-level proposals should include all materials relevant to the new program/proposed changes, including supporting documentation from other academic units impacted by these changes.
All program and applicable accreditation requirements should be listed .
The Kuali ﬁelds for program proposals should include courses impacted by changes.
Course and Program Overlap Overlap is when a newly proposed or modiﬁed course/program intersects with the content of an existing course or program.
The amount of overlap might range from small (the topics of a single class) to approaching virtual duplication.
Proposers and curriculum approval committees can use search features within Kuali to compare other current and proposed courses/programs for potential overlap.

When CASC recognizes potential overlap, they will ask the course proposer and department/instructor to consult regarding the degree and signiﬁcance of overlap.
Even with substantial replication in content, there might be key differences in approach.
As CASC cannot be experts in all disciplines, we request that the proposer and faculty for the existing course/program work together.
This collaboration can be documented in a statement communicating the resolution to CASC.
If this collaboration cannot occur, CASC exercises its best judgment regarding student beneﬁt.
Note: overlap issues can also be addressed on the Faculty Senate ﬂoor or even at ﬁnal approval with the President.
We also encourage colleges to check for overlap themselves.
Starting in Fall 2025, CASC’s ‘Proposed Temporary and Permanent Courses/Programs’ email will be distributed at the end of the last full week of each month.
We encourage each college’s curriculum committee to meet during the ﬁrst full week of each month and, as part of their deliberations, carefully consider all newly proposed offerings in that CASC newsletter for potential overlap.

Any overlapping courses/programs should be reported to Genviéve Spitale ( genvieve.spitale@uri.edu ); the course/program will not be reviewed until the originating and overlapping colleges agree in writing that either the original proposal or a revised version can move forward for CASC/Gen Ed/Grad Council consideration.

2 The School of Education currently offers a Bachelor of Arts degree in Secondary Education, with multiple tracks reflecting various specializations.
Since its inception, the World Language Education Program has been one of these tracks (the other tracks are English, History/Social Studies, Mathematics, and Science).
Upon graduation, stude nts in the Secondary Education Program obtain certification to teach at the High School level (grades 7-12).
Upon the completion of an additional course and a teaching practicum at a Middle School, students in this existing program also have the option to obtain a Middle School extension, a credential that allows them to teach in grades 5-8 in any Rhode Island elementary, middle, or junior high school.
Recently the Rhode Island Department of Education changed the World Language teacher certification system.
Due to these changes, graduates from our current Secondary Education – World Language program are now certified to teach in Rhode Island at all levels of elementary, middle, and secondary education (grades PK-12).

The new program proposal is intended to address the changes in Rhode Island certification regulations, which will require significant changes (over 25%) to the requirements for our current BA in Secondary Education with a specialization in World Languages, effectively transforming it into a BA in World Language Education-All Grades.
In the proposed new program, students will take a variety of existing EDC courses in Elementary Education, Early Childhood Education, Secondary Education, and Teaching English as a Second Language / Bilingual Education concentrations so that, upon graduation, they will be more versatile and highly employable educators who are better prepared to teach effectively in a wider variety of educational settings.
The new program will educate our students to become reflective teachers committed to global citizenship, social justice, and multicultural education.

Our program of study, based on current research and best practices, has been carefully crafted to provide our teacher candidates with ample opportunities to learn about different professional contexts and acquire knowledge about learning theory (social, emotional, and academic), and how to address the individualized needs of diverse learners.
Through a variety of hands-on teaching experiences at PK-12 academic settings our candidates will have the opportunity to apply what they learn in URI courses in culturally responsive practices but also to learn to work with and from practicing teachers.
The standard program of study that our candidates will follow will allow them to graduate from URI with a double major in Education and in a Foreign Language.1 Students will develop their teaching skills and acquire knowledge through coursework that focuses on teaching and learning at different developmental levels, and on cutting-edge second language acquisition theories.
Our program will help teacher candidates develop the necessary confidence and experience to effectively engage with a diverse group of students in a variety of educational settings.

Upon completion of our program and after successfully completing the licensure tests, our well- prepared graduates will be ready to apply for the Rhode Island World Language teacher certification in grades K-12.

What is the economic need and workforce data related to the program?
One of the purposes of the new program is to attract, retain, and graduate more teachers from multicultural, multilingual, historically marginalized, and under -represented groups in the education profession.
The inclusion of coursework in Bilingual Education and Teaching English as a Second Language aims to attract and harness the unique talents and lived experiences of students from our important local and regional multilingual communities.
In addition to this, the RI

4 Department of Education, through the work of the Rhode Island Council on Elementary and Secondary Education, is currently in the process of changing the state’s high school graduation requirements.
Among the proposed changes to the system, students will be required to take a minimum of two years of study of the same language in order to successfully graduate from high school.
This change has the potential to strengthen the general pipeline of candidates for our proposed World Language Education-All Grades program.
Finally, given both the regional and national shortage of world language educators, as evidenced by the 100% employment rates of graduates from our existing program and the high percentage of new language teachers who are being hired through an emergency certification process, the demand for well-qualified K-12 world language educators is high and the urgent need for this program is clear.

Explain how the program is consistent with the published role and mission of the institution and how it is related to the institution’s academic planning.
Embracing Rhode Island ’s heritage of independent thought, we value: As stated in the URI’s mission statement, our institutional values: o Creativity and scholarship o Diversity, fairness, and respect o Engaged learning and civic involvement o Intellectual and ethical leadership The program that we are proposing is not only consistent with those key guiding principles, but it can have a significant impact by strengthening those values in our learning community and RI society.

Our program, based on rigorous scholarship, will help to shape the face of education in the state.
The RI Department of Education is about to approve new high school graduation requirements that include the study of the same World Language for two years.
A new WL Education Program could potentially attract more heritage speakers into the teaching profession.
This will increase the diversity among faculty in our schools and will provide multilingual students with role models with whom they can identify.
We anticipate that our graduates will become

5 leaders and advocates in multicultural and multilingual education: from a very early stage we will foster collaboration with regional associations such as the RI Foreign Language Association (RIFLA) or the Coalition for a Multilingual RI.
As a matter of fact, I currently serve as university liaison for RIFLA and Sarah Steverman (current RIFLA President) has been a guest presenter in my EDC 485 (Seminar of teaching) class.
The new proposed program of study will help our graduates develop their intercultural skills and acquire a “glocal” perspective, that is, the capacity to understand how local and global events are interconnected and the effects that they have on each other.

Estimate the projected impact of this program on other public higher education institutions in Rhode Island (e.g. loss of students or revenues), provide a rationale for the assumptions made in the projections, and indicate the manner in which the other public institutions were consulted in developing the projections.
Have you communicated with other institutions about the development of this program and have any concerns been raised related to role, scope, and mission or duplication.
Our program will not create any new competition to attract students that will be detrimental for other RI institutions of higher education, as the intent of the program is to adjust an already existing academic offering to the new certification reality implemented by the RI Department of Education.
The impact of the program will not be noticeable to other WL Education Programs around the state, only to the URI students that would benefit from a curriculum that better adjusts to their future professional needs.

To the best of my knowledge there are four other higher ed institutions in RI that offer World Language Education programs: Salve Regina, Rhode Island College, Providence College and Roger Williams University.
None of these programs is new: such programs have been in place for at least 10 years.
In all those cases, the original World Language programs were part of the Secondary Education programs, just one of the multiple tracks that students could take.
Two of those institutions have already taken steps to adapt to the new RIDE certification reality.
Recently, in both Salve Regina and RIC the World Language Program has become independent.
According to the information listed on their websites, the World Language Education program is still a track of the Secondary Education Program in the cases of both Providence College (<https://academics.providence.edu/secondary-education/>) and Roger Williams University (<https://www.rwu.edu/undergraduate/academics/programs/secondary-education>).

The new URI World Language Education program will fill a void that currently exists in the world language teacher preparation programs by focusing on providing more comprehensive preparation to our candidates so they can be effective teachers at the elementary and secondary levels, and it will allow us to continue being the leader in preparing future world language educators in the state of RI.

How does this program align to academic programs at other institutions?
Upon examination of the program of study of existing academic programs at other institutions, one can say that, in most cases their curriculum still follows very closely the Secondary Education program.

This is true even in the case of Salve Regina, an institution in which the World Language Program has become independent.2 In the case of RIC, our program of study will make a slightly increased emphasis on Second Language Teaching and will include courses that focus on early learners.3 The proposed program will include more offerings (existing courses already taught regularly by the School of Education faculty) that will prepare our students to teach at the PK-5 grades and provide a stronger foundation in theories and methodologies of teaching Second Languages.
Salve Regina currently offers two tracks in their World Language Education program: French and Spanish.
RIC currently offers three tracks in their World Language Education program (French, Portuguese, and Spanish).
Providence Colleges offers three tracks (French, Italian, and Spanish) and Roger Williams University offers five (French, German, Italian, Latin, and Spanish).
URI is the only institution that offers a World Language Education track in Chinese and the only public institution to offer tracks in German, Italian, and Latin.
